rationale: This Stanford Puzzle build is a tiny (3.9 KB text, 9 functions) recursive-backtracking benchmark whose hot functions (Puzzle, Trial) dominate execution, so reverse-engineering resistance must be bought mostly with control-flow and structural transformations whose per-execution overhead is low or amortized. SPLIT and SUB get the strongest green light: they are nearly free at runtime, compose well with other passes, and meaningfully raise static-analysis effort on small functions like Fit and Remove, so their cost/risk weights are kept minimal. FLA and IBR are the primary security levers against the large control-flow-heavy Puzzle and Trial (dispatch loops and indirect branching defeat trivial CFG recovery) and are strongly favored, but their RuntimeCost weights stay elevated so the selector avoids stacking them on deeply recursive hot paths. BCF is treated as a conditional filler: useful bogus-edge diversity on cold functions, but with the highest RuntimeCost and a notable CorrectnessRisk weight it will be filtered out wherever the profile shows tight loops or high dynamic frequency. ICALL and IGV are enabled with moderate weights to add inter-procedural indirection diversity — cheap on a 9-function program where call sites are few — yet their runtime and risk weights are high enough to spare the recursion-heavy call chains (Trial/Puzzle) where indirect dispatch would compound overhead. SizeCost weights are uniformly low because the binary is minuscule and growth of even 3-5x is acceptable here; the binding constraint is runtime, which is why the cost dimensions are concentrated on RuntimeCost and, secondarily, CorrectnessRisk to guarantee the benchmark still produces correct results.
